strengths: Timely and important problem: safety of LLM-based search agents exposed to unreliable web content is a genuinely under-explored threat surface, and the paper motivates it with both a real-world anecdote and two original in-the-wild experiments (4.3% of 8,933 search results flagged as probable content farms; 46/1,000 differential-testing cases where search results flipped agent stances).

Well-designed and well-justified threat model: benign queries, at most one injected unreliable website, agent-agnostic (not tailored per-agent), with the threat placed after LLM knowledge cutoffs. The careful argument in Section E.5 for why simulation-based testing is preferable to user-driven measurement or blackhat SEO is convincing from both ethical and scientific standpoints.

Thorough experimental coverage: three representative scaffolds (search workflow, tool calling, deep research) and 15 backend LLMs, yielding a broad and informative comparison (Table 2) with clear findings—e.g., reasoning models and deep-research scaffolds improve resilience, misinformation is the hardest risk, injection shows lowest ASR.

Strong validation of configuration choices: ablations over injection position, per-website token limit, timestamp persistence, website generator choice, search result count, and reasoning effort (Figures 6, 8, 9, 10). The checklist-assisted safety evaluator is validated against two human annotators on 200 samples with high agreement (95-98%).

Useful downstream analyses beyond raw benchmarking: defense evaluation showing reminder prompting is largely ineffective while filtering halves ASR, identification of a knowledge-action gap, and an insightful CoT-monitoring case study explaining why GPT-5(-mini) is markedly safer (source-credibility discussion, selective adoption).

Good reproducibility and ethics treatment: public code and test cases via anonymous URL, all prompts released (Section G), caching of search results for cross-agent fairness, explicit ethics and reproducibility statements, and a thoughtful limitations section covering proprietary system exclusion, single search service, benchmark scale, and omitted efficiency metrics.
weaknesses: Potential selection bias inflating ASR: the 'attainability' filter retains only test cases where a dry-run with the baseline agent (Qwen3-8B) confirms the target consequence occurs. This biases the benchmark toward cases that at least one agent already fails on, so headline ASR figures (e.g., 90.5%) likely overstate the average vulnerability an arbitrary attack would achieve. The paper does not quantify how much of the reported ASR stems from this selection.

Circularity in the automated pipeline: test cases, unreliable websites, and safety judgments are all produced/checked by LLMs (o4-mini as generator, GPT-4.1-mini as website generator and judge). The judge's agreement with humans is only validated on 200 samples from just three models under one scaffold, and the generator/judge/agents share model families, which may correlate errors; the full 300-case set is not independently human-audited.

External validity of the simulated threat: injected websites are LLM-generated and the authors concede stealthiness was not a design principle; the reported 44.2% filter recall may therefore underestimate realistic risk, but conversely, synthetic sites mixed into cached Google results differ from genuinely ranked adversarial content, so the sim-to-real gap is not fully quantified.

Reliance on LLM-as-judge for both safety (boolean) and helpfulness (1-5 scale); the helpfulness evaluation is not human-validated at all, yet conclusions such as 'HS_manip (91.6) exceeds HS_benign (90.7)' and the Pareto-optimality claim rest on it, and small numerical differences (less than one point) are interpreted substantively.

Modest scale and statistical depth: 300 test cases (60 per risk), 3 stochastic trials per case, no confidence intervals or significance tests reported, and single snapshot timestamps (Sep 9/17, 2025) mean several fine-grained cross-model comparisons may not be robust.

Novelty is incremental relative to adjacent work: RAG poisoning and unsafe-web-search studies (e.g., PoisonedRAG, Luo et al. 2025) already establish that corrupted retrieved content misleads LLMs; the contribution is primarily consolidating this into an automated, agent-level benchmark rather than a fundamentally new insight or method.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant problem: safety of LLM-based search agents under unreliable web content is an important threat surface that existing agent-safety benchmarks cover only narrowly.

The paper is thorough in validating its own experimental choices: ablations on injection position, token limits, timestamps, website generator choice, and search-result count (Section C), plus a human agreement study of the checklist-assisted judge (96–98% agreement over 200 samples).

The simulation-based injection design is a reasonable, harmless alternative to real-world SEO manipulation, and the threat model (benign queries, at most one injected site, agent-agnostic attacks) is stated explicitly and conservatively.

Evaluation coverage is broad: three scaffolds (search workflow, tool calling, deep research) and fifteen backend LLMs, with useful analyses such as the knowledge–action gap, defense effectiveness (reminder vs. filtering), and the GPT-5-mini CoT monitoring case study.
Honest and detailed limitations/ethics discussion; code, prompts, and test cases are released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core technique is essentially single-document retrieval poisoning with LLM-generated synthetic pages, which is close to existing RAG corruption attacks (e.g., PoisonedRAG) and agentic safety benchmarks; the claimed distinction from RAG safety (dynamic web) motivates the setting but not a new method.

The evaluation pipeline has several LLM-in-the-loop weaknesses that are only partially mitigated: test cases are generated and filtered using models (o4-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, Qwen3-8B) that also appear among the evaluated agents (circularity risk), and the judge validation covers only 200 of ~hundreds of thousands of judgments from a narrow response mixture.

Attainability filtering uses a single weak baseline (Qwen3-8B) dry run, so the 300 curated cases are biased toward vulnerabilities of one model family; very low retention rates for Harm (6.9%) and Injection (6.8%) raise questions about whether the generator can actually target adversarial risks at all, despite these being headlined risk categories.

Some headline results are less alarming than presented: the highest ASR (90.5%) comes from a search-workflow scaffold on non-reasoning models that passively consume search snippets; GPT-5 with tool calling achieves ~5% ASR, suggesting the benchmark may saturate quickly for frontier systems.

The indirect prompt injection instantiation (Figure 16) is a trivially detectable marker-string instruction, which partly explains the low injection ASR and weakens the claim of broad adversarial risk coverage; the generated websites also explicitly omit stealth, as the authors themselves admit when interpreting the filtering defense.

Conclusions are largely intuitive (models repeat retrieved content; reasoning and multi-source cross-validation help), so the paper's main value is the benchmark artifact rather than new understanding; 300 cases (60 per risk) is a modest scale for a benchmark whose central contribution is the resource.

Presentation issues: an ICML submission whose ethics statement pledges adherence to the 'ICLR Code of Ethics'; several findings sections read more like a product-style report than rigorous analysis (e.g., 'Pareto-optimal balance' claimed from a handful of GPT-5 data points).

strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem: the paper clearly establishes that search agents inherit the unreliability of Internet-sourced search results, supported by two systematic in-the-wild motivating experiments (4.3% content-farm prevalence across 8,933 sites; 46/1,000 stance shifts in health-related differential testing) rather than relying solely on the anecdote in Figure 1.

The simulation-based threat model is carefully reasoned and conservative: benign queries only, at most one injected unreliable website, agent-agnostic test cases, injection only in the first search round, and injection at the 'Last' position (the least adversarial of the tested positions), which strengthens the credibility of the reported high ASRs rather than overstating risk (Section 3.1, Appendix C).

Comprehensive evaluation: three representative scaffolds (search workflow, tool calling, deep research) across 15 backend LLMs (7 proprietary, 8 open-source), with 300 test cases over five risk types, three repetitions per case, and cached search results for fairness and reproducibility.

Unusually thorough ablation and validation of the testing methodology itself: injection position (Fig. 8), per-website token limit, temporal persistence of the injected site (Fig. 9), website generator choice, and a human agreement study of the checklist-assisted safety evaluator (96-98% agreement between two human annotators and GPT-4.1-mini on 200 samples). This addresses the main circularity concern of LLM-generated tests being judged by LLMs.

Actionable analysis beyond raw numbers: defense evaluation showing reminder prompting is largely ineffective while filtering halves ASR (44.2% recall), the safety/helpfulness Pareto analysis, the knowledge-action gap finding, and the GPT-5-mini CoT-monitoring case study (Section D) that offers mechanistic insight rather than mere benchmarking.

Good research ethics treatment: simulation avoids real-world SEO harm, offensive content is quarantined with disclaimers, and human annotator well-being is discussed. Reproducibility is strong: anonymous code, test cases, and all prompts (Section G) are released, and limitations (proprietary systems, single search provider, benchmark scale, missing efficiency metrics) are honestly stated.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on LLM-generated artifacts at every stage (o4-mini for test generation, GPT-4.1-mini for websites and judging). The human validation of the safety judge covers only 200 responses from the search-workflow setting with three models; the helpfulness evaluator and test cases from other scaffolds/risk types are not human-validated, so some ASR/HS numbers may embed generator or judge bias.

Benchmark scale is modest (300 cases, 60 per risk), and the very low retention rates for adversarial risks (6.8-6.9%) suggest the curation pipeline systematically filters toward certain case styles, which may under-represent harder or stealthier adversarial scenarios -- a concern the authors themselves acknowledge via the detection-recall discussion.

The 'unreliable website' generation is non-stealthy by design; the demonstrated filter defense (44.2% recall) exploits this. The paper is honest about this, but it means headline ASRs characterize only the low end of threat sophistication and the defense conclusions may not transfer to more realistic adversaries.

Only Google Search (via Serper) is studied, and proprietary deployed search agents (ChatGPT Search, Gemini, Perplexity) are excluded due to tool-hooking constraints, so the paper cannot speak directly about the systems most users actually face; the extrapolation to proprietary systems in Section E.2 is plausible but unverified.

Some in-the-wild evidence is thin or unverified: the 4.3% content-farm rate rests on GPT-4.1 labeling without human spot-checks, and the 46/1,000 stance-shift figure is small and only manually reviewed qualitatively.

Findings such as 'reasoning models are more resilient' and the GPT-5-mini CoT analysis are correlational and partly confounded (e.g., knowledge cutoff, post-training differences); the authors appropriately hedge, but several summary claims in the introduction are stated more strongly than the evidence supports.

Results are tied to a specific snapshot (Sep 2025) of live search results and models; while timestamp handling is ablated, the benchmark's absolute ASR values will decay, limiting long-term comparability.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important safety question: how LLM-based search agents behave when search results contain unreliable content. The agent-centric framing (benign queries, unreliable results injected via a hooked search tool) is well-motivated by real-world incidents and two in-the-wild motivating studies.

Comprehensive and transparent evaluation: 300 test cases across 5 risk types, 3 scaffolds, and 17 LLMs, with extensive ablations of red-teaming configurations (injection position, token limits, timestamps, generator choice, injection round) that validate the design choices rather than leaving them arbitrary.

Careful treatment of measurement validity: checklist-assisted LLM-as-a-judge safety evaluation is validated against human annotators (≥95% agreement), integrity checks show near-zero false-positive ASR without injection (0.81% average), and differential filtering (attainability/integrity) guards against infeasible test cases inflating vulnerability claims.

Ethically responsible design: simulation-based injection avoids real-world SEO manipulation, the threat model is conservative (single injected website, appended last, first round only), and the impact statement discusses ethics thoroughly.

Useful analysis beyond benchmarking: findings on scaffold effects (deep research improves safety), the knowledge-action gap, defense evaluation (reminder prompting largely ineffective; filtering reduces ASR by ~half), and tiered test-case difficulty for continuous supervision add practical value for agent developers.
Strong reproducibility posture: code, dataset, prompts (Appendix M), model details, and decoding configurations are released or documented.
weaknesses: Circularity/contamination risks in the pipeline: o4-mini generates the test cases and GPT-4.1-mini generates websites and serves as the safety judge, while both models are also evaluated as agents. The agent-agnostic threat model mitigates this, but shared-family biases (judge leniency, generator-test alignment) are not fully analyzed; the judge validation covers only 200 responses from three search-workflow agents.

The central 'vulnerability' interpretation is debatable: a search agent that faithfully relays or summarizes retrieved content (misinformation, ads) is arguably performing its function; whether the correct behavior is to discount single-source claims is a design judgment. The paper asserts a normative safety standard (critical utilization of retrieved content) without engaging with the counter-position, so high ASR may partly measure capability/skepticism rather than safety failure per se.

Threat model realism: the injected website is appended last and known to the tester with a checklist tailored to it; findings on injection position (first-position ASR of 94.6%) and persuasiveness ablations show the reported ASRs are sensitive to configuration, so the headline numbers (e.g., 90.5% ASR) should be read as lower-bound-style estimates rather than deployment-risk measurements.

Modest novelty relative to very recent concurrent work (Luo et al. 2025; Ou et al. 2025/Crest-Search); the differentiation (agent-level vs. system-level, broader risk coverage, simulation-based injection) is real but incremental, and low retention rates for the two adversarial risk types (~6.8–6.9%) suggest these portions are hard to curate reliably.

Statistical reporting is thin in places: 60 test cases per risk × 3 trials without confidence intervals or variance reporting in Table 1, and comparisons between models/scaffolds (e.g., GPT-5-mini vs. GPT-5) are sometimes based on differences that may fall within sampling noise.

Defense analysis is limited to two simple baselines (reminder, filtering with 44.2% recall); the conclusion that 'common defenses offer limited protection' would be stronger with at least one stronger, more realistic defense (e.g., source-verification scaffolds or ensemble cross-checking), though this is acknowledged as future work.

Evaluation is limited to Google Search with cached results and excludes proprietary deep-research systems, which the authors acknowledge; this limits external validity of the safety claims for deployed systems.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant problem: safety of LLM-based search agents exposed to unreliable web results is an under-explored threat surface, and the paper motivates it with both a real-world incident and two small in-the-wild observations (content-farm prevalence, stance shifts on health queries).

Comprehensive empirical scope: 300 test cases across five risk categories, three agent scaffolds, and 17 backend LLMs (9 proprietary, 8 open-source), with results reported in a large, readable main table.

Unusually thorough validation and ablation effort for a benchmark paper: seven configuration ablations (injection position, token limit, timestamp, generator choice, injection round, persuasiveness, open-source test generator), tiered difficulty filtering, ASR_benign integrity checks (global average 0.81%), and a human study validating the checklist-assisted evaluator (95-98% agreement).

Reasonable and clearly argued threat model (benign queries, at most one injected website, agent-agnostic), and a well-justified simulation-based design that avoids harming real users, with an explicit impact statement and released code/data/prompts supporting reproducibility.

Useful downstream findings: reminder prompting is largely ineffective, filtering helps only partially, scaffolds matter as much as models, and the knowledge-action gap analysis (GPT-4.1-mini detects unreliability when tasked but fails to act on it) is an interesting observation.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core technique is LLM-prompt-chained test case generation plus injecting one LLM-generated website into search results. Crafting adversarial/misleading documents to fool LLMs is well studied (the paper itself cites Chen & Shu 2024, PoisonedRAG, etc.), and the closest works (Luo et al. 2025, Ou et al. 2025) are differentiated only incrementally (broader risk taxonomy, agent-centric framing).

Threat-model mismatch at the heart of the headline claims: the paper frames the threat as incidental unreliability (content farms, SEO noise) but the injected website is a strong-LLM-generated, query-tailored, deliberately misleading page. This is closer to a targeted misinformation attack than to naturally occurring unreliable results, so the reported ASRs (up to 90.5%) likely overstate the risk from 'unreliable search results' as motivated in Observation 1.

Potential evaluator/generator circularity and bias: o4-mini generates the tests, GPT-4.1-mini generates the websites and serves as both safety and helpfulness judge, and the filtering baseline is also an LLM. Human validation covers only 200 responses, from only three models under a single scaffold, annotated solely by the authors, so the ~95% agreement may not generalize to the full 17-model, 3-scaffold space or to borderline judgments.

External validity is narrow: only Google Search (via Serper) is tested; search results are cached and injected at a fixed 'Last' position for reproducibility; proprietary deep-research products are excluded entirely, yet the paper's conclusions concern 'search agents' broadly.

Some evidence quality issues: retention rates of 6.8-6.9% for the two adversarial risk types suggest substantial generation fragility; anomalies like GPT-oss-120b's HS_benign of 60.4 (vs. ~95 for all peers) are visible in Table 1 but never explained; the 300-case benchmark is modest in size.

Presentation is verbose and somewhat promotional, with many results deferred to a very long appendix; minor sloppiness (e.g., 'dndirect prompt injection' in Figure 16) undermines confidence in final polish. The core contribution is empirical and benchmark-like, which may be a modest fit for the main research track without stronger methodological novelty or a more validated measurement pipeline.

strengths: Clear and timely problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine, under-studied threat surface (unreliable Internet-sourced search results compromising search agents) and convincingly distinguishes it from RAG poisoning (Appendix A), which strengthens the motivation beyond 'RAG safety with a new name.'

Well-designed red-teaming methodology: the three-step test generation workflow, differential-testing-based quality filtering (attainability + integrity), and checklist-assisted safety evaluation are thoughtfully engineered, and the near-zero ASR under benign conditions (0.81% average, Table 10) provides good evidence that observed failures are causally attributable to the injected unreliable website rather than judge over-flagging or inherently unsafe queries.

Empirically comprehensive: 300 test cases across five risk types, three scaffolds, and 17 LLMs, with 3 runs per case. The paper also validates the safety evaluator against human annotators (96-98% agreement), ablates seven testing configurations (injection position, token limit, timestamp, generator choice, injection round, persuasiveness, test generator), and demonstrates continuous supervision via tiered filtering against stronger baselines (Table 8).

Useful actionable findings: scaffold design matters as much as the backend LLM (90.5% -> 77.8% -> 57.4% ASR for GPT-4.1-mini), reminder prompting is largely ineffective, the knowledge-action gap analysis, and the CoT monitoring case study (Appendix H) offer concrete guidance for agent developers.

Ethical treatment is careful: simulation-based testing avoids real-world SEO manipulation, the threat model is explicitly conservative (benign queries, single injected site, first-round injection), disclaimers and responsible-release practices are present, and the impact statement addresses reviewer-facing content concerns.
Reproducibility support is good: prompts are fully disclosed (Appendix M), open-source test generation is shown feasible (Table 7), and code/dataset release is stated.
weaknesses: Potential circularity and single-judge dependence: GPT-4.1-mini serves simultaneously as website generator, safety evaluator, helpfulness evaluator, and filtering defense. While the human validation (200 samples, two annotators) is reassuring, it covers only the search-workflow scaffold and three models; judge reliability for tool-calling and deep-research trajectories (longer, multi-turn, more ambiguous outputs) is unverified, and the checklist is described as 'not strict but highly expected to be met,' leaving some room for leniency that could inflate ASR.

Sim-to-real gap is acknowledged but not quantified: the injected website is guaranteed to be topically relevant, always appended to results, and LLM-generated. Observation 2's stance-shift experiment (46/1000) suggests real-world impact is far lower in frequency than the 60-90% ASRs reported under controlled injection; the paper's argument that this measures a 'risk lower bound' is reasonable but the practical prevalence of the threat (given Google's safety investments, which the authors themselves note) remains uncertain.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals despite three stochastic runs; differences of a few percentage points between closely ranked models (e.g., GPT-5 vs. GPT-5-mini, Claude vs. GPT-5) may not be meaningful, yet ranking claims are made from them.

Benchmark scale is modest (300 cases, 60 per risk, with only 6.8-6.9% retention for the two adversarial risks), and coverage is limited to a single search service (Google via Serper), which the limitations section honestly discusses but which narrows the generality of conclusions about 'search services' broadly.

Some framing leans promotional: comparisons with the closest concurrent work (Luo et al., 2025; Ou et al., 2025) are self-positioned favorably on scope and risk coverage without head-to-head empirical comparison, and several headline claims (e.g., 'substantial vulnerabilities') could benefit from more careful qualification given the conservative evaluation setup.

Helpfulness evaluation (HS) is secondary and under-validated: the claim that unsafe responses 'still appear useful' rests on a 1-5 LLM rating whose reliability is not human-validated, and the interpretation that HS_manip > HS_benign indicates 'subtle unsafe influence' has alternative explanations.
